For the uninitiated, the crack spreads refers to the price differential between the product and the underlying crude price. 

For US, I used Heating Oil contracts against WTI. Oct WTI swap is around 95$/bbl, so the flatprice of diesel in US is more than 200$/bbl.

For the European market, I used ICE GO swaps against Brent. Oct Brent swap is around 100$/bbl, so flatprice of diesel in Europe is around 190$/bbl.

Singapore markets are similar to the Europe side, marked against Brent (some mark cracks against Dubai too). For this exercise, the flatprice of diesel in SIngapore is around 180$/bbl.

This also shows you the divergence between East and West spreads. Diesel in the East is weaker than the Atlantic Basin. But it is still very, very strong.

Lots of questions and confused numbers out there, so to clarify:

Saudi Arabia's East-West Pipeline has a theoretical max capacity of 7 MMbpd.

The highest sustained Saudi West Coast export pace we've seen during the conflict is ~5.5 MMbpd, which is 3.5 MMbpd higher than the ~2 MMbpd prewar norm.

So 3.5 MMbpd was the incremental swing from the Gulf to the Red Sea.

That 5.5 MMbpd export pace sank sharply in August following Houthi maritime ban, but had begun climbing back—latest at ~4 MMbpd.

So if the East-West Pipeline is down for long and the Saudis run out of West Coast inventories, then the hit to the market today vs last week is about 4 MMbpd (~4%)

(Saudi West Coast total liquids exports below, via Kpler)

My last tweet caught unprompted traction—and cue the usual bad faith replies in the mentions—but Saudi Energy Ministry just confirmed the kinetic Houthi hit. 

Narrative pivot. it's no longer if, it's strictly the outage duration.

It appears this was a localized hit on a pump station rather than a sweeping strike spanning hundreds of kilometers. Damage assessment at the pad aside, I’m fading the idea that this flow impairment drags out.

As far as I know, there are several contingency plays for such events and I spoke with midstream engineers today. Here are the primary workarounds:

1) Heavily injecting Drag Reducing Agents(DRA). This is one of the fastest emergency levers available. At the fully operational pump station immediately upstream of the damaged site, operators inject large volumes of DRA—specialized polymer chemical additives. This kills boundary layer turbulence inside the pipe, collapsing frictional head loss.

Less frictional drag means the upstream head pushes barrels significantly further down the line. It's the standard emergency lever to claw back 10% to 40%+ of lost nameplate flow almost immediately without laying an inch of steel.

2) Hydraulic bypass & pressure rebalancing. Isolate the fried booster and redline the surrounding stations. Upstream station pegs its discharge pressure right against the pipe's MAOP ceiling.

Simultaneously the downstream station dials down its suction pressure floor to the absolute limit. Blowing out that delta-P forces the crude across the dead zone via pure brute-force hydraulics.

3) Tactical hardware deployments. Aramco can roll out trailer-mounted mobile pump skids (diesel/gas turbine-driven) straight to the site to patch the lost pressure head.

Alternatively close the ESDVs, isolate the manifold and crack the station bypass loop to free-flow barrels around the blast zone. If there are looped parallel segments or pipeline interties nearby, they can divert batches around the pinch point.

4) Lastly, adjusting crude viscosity—such as blending lower-viscosity crudes or condensates—is technically a method, but Saudi Arabia is not a light crude/condensate powerhouse, and maintaining crude quality integrity makes this practically unviable, so let's write that off.

Even running every emergency trick, some capacity haircut is baked in. Terminal hubs and refiners at Yanbu will just burn through regional storage buffers to bridge the delta while crews turn wrenches.

In conclusion, provided there are no follow-up attacks, these stopgap measures should preserve substantial throughput while repair crews work around the clock. The Saudis are about as prepared for this specific operational headache as anyone can be.

The binary risk is follow-up kinetic strikes. If not, this won't morph into a full-blown physical catastrophe. But as we all know, E/W pipeline aside global macro crude setup is already...

#Agriculture: US grains futures rounded off a volatile week that saw weather, war, profit-taking and elevated speculative positioning all influence prices at various stages. The week ended on a sour note following Friday’s September WASDE report, leaving wheat down 3.8%, corn 1.9% lower and soybeans down 1.4% on the week.

September is the first month in which USDA statisticians incorporate field samples into their corn and soybean yield estimates, alongside farmer surveys and satellite data. Corn production was estimated at 15.8 billion bushels with a yield of 178.5 bushels per acre, both sharply below August’s 16 billion and 180.7 bpa forecasts, but slightly above trade expectations. Soybeans delivered a more bearish surprise, with production raised to 4.535 billion bushels and yield to 52.8 bpa, both above August estimates and market expectations.

Ending stocks also offered limited support. US corn stocks were lowered from August but remained above expectations at 1.567 billion bushels, while soybean stocks at 310 million bushels were 5% above the trade estimate. Global wheat stocks provided another bearish surprise, rising to 276.3 million tonnes versus 273.2 million expected.

The reaction was amplified by crowded positioning. Ahead of the report, managed money accounts held a record one million-contract net long across the six major grain futures, following almost 600,000 contracts of net buying in just three weeks from mid-August. With bullish expectations already elevated, the WASDE offered little fresh fuel to sustain the rally, leaving the market vulnerable to profit-taking.

An index tracking global #container spot rates held steady for a third week, but a closer look reveals a widening divergence between transpacific and Asia–Europe routes.

The Drewry composite index rose just 0.3% in the past week to USD 4,476 per 40-foot container, around where it has traded for the past three weeks and leaving the year-to-date increase at 102%.

Beneath the headline figure, however, transpacific rates continue to surge. Shanghai-to-Los Angeles reached another post-pandemic high at USD 7,352, while Shanghai-to-New York climbed to USD 9,726. Both routes are now up close to 200% year to date, propelled by resilient demand, drought-induced Panama Canal bottlenecks and continued Red Sea transit diversions.

Asia–Europe rates, meanwhile, eased further amid softer import volumes and recovering capacity as some Red Sea routes resume. The benchmark Shanghai-to-Rotterdam rate slipped to USD 3,997 per container, leaving it up a comparatively modest 55% since the start of the year.

The IEA cut its oil-demand forecast as the prolonged Iran war forces consumers to adjust to reduced supply and elevated prices. It now expects global oil demand to fall by 2.5 million b/d this year, a 940,000 b/d deeper contraction than previously forecast and the largest annual decline since the 2020 pandemic. Despite this demand destruction, the agency sees an even deeper supply shortfall, with disrupted flows outweighing weaker consumption, inventories drawing at record rates and the return of a supply surplus pushed into 2027.
